title: Observation geometry for uncertainty-aware Hamiltonian inference and experimental design in quantum magnets
authors: Roy Liu, Venugopal Ranganathan, David Dahlbom, Shizhou Xu, Tianyu Zhang, Yuan Ni, Daniel M. Pajerowski, Garrett Granroth, Thomas Strohmer, Matthew B. Stone, Andrew F. May, Mark D. Lumsden, Joshua J. Turner, Yongqiang Cheng, Zhantao Chen
abstract: Determining microscopic interactions from spectroscopic and scattering measurements is central to understanding quantum materials, yet it often remains unclear which interactions can be reliably revealed by the available experimental data and how additional experimental modalities should be designed to resolve the remaining ambiguities. Here we present an artificial intelligence-enabled framework for uncertainty-aware Hamiltonian inference and adaptive experimental design. By combining Hamiltonian-conditioned neural surrogates with Bayesian inference and observation geometry, the framework characterizes how measurements constrain Hamiltonian parameter space, quantifies the identifiability of microscopic interactions, and propagates posterior uncertainty directly in the physical Hamiltonian parameter space rather than an abstract learned representation. Using multimodal powder and single-crystal inelastic neutron scattering measurements of the quantum magnet NiPS$_{3}$, we demonstrate physically interpretable Hamiltonian inference, modality-aware uncertainty quantification, and adaptive experimental design. The framework provides a general strategy for uncertainty-aware microscopic characterization and multimodal experimental design across quantum materials.
summary: This work presents an AI-enabled framework that tackles the difficult inverse problem of determining quantum magnetic interactions from experimental spectra. By treating different measurements (single-crystal vs. powder INS) as geometric constraints on the parameter space, it quantifies which interactions are uniquely identifiable and guides adaptive data collection strategies for improved characterization.
main_problem: The core challenge is determining microscopic magnetic interactions (Hamiltonian parameters) from complex, multimodal spectroscopic data, as the inverse problem is often ill-posed.
main_result: The proposed framework successfully performs uncertainty-aware Hamiltonian inference by quantifying how different measurement modalities constrain the parameter space using observation geometry.
method: It employs an AI surrogate model (INRs) trained on simulated spectra to map Hamiltonian parameters to measured spectral data, integrating this with Bayesian inference.
model_or_system: The study focuses on quantum magnets, specifically $	ext{NiPS}_3$, modeled by a spin Hamiltonian involving exchange couplings and anisotropies. Measurements utilize Inelastic Neutron Scattering (INS) from both single-crystal and powder samples.
key_observables: Dynamical structure factor $S(Q, \omega)$, inferred Hamiltonian parameters ($	heta$), spectral distinguishability metrics, and the local/global Gram matrix characterizing parameter sensitivity.
important_parameters: Hamiltonian coupling constants ($J_{ij}, A_x, A_z$) defining the magnetic interactions; momentum transfer $\mathbf{Q}$ and energy $\omega$.
main_assumptions: The framework assumes that spectral distinguishability is governed by the geometry induced by the forward map ($	heta ightarrow S$), rather than Euclidean distance in parameter space. Source separation for powder data introduces model-dependent estimation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the setup of INS measurements (single-crystal vs. powder), the AI surrogate architecture, and detailed spectral discrepancy maps showing how different measurement modalities constrain the Hamiltonian parameters via geometry analysis.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the ill-posed nature of inverse problems in quantum magnetism. It then introduces the AI framework using INRs to model spectra from a given Hamiltonian. The core methodology involves characterizing parameter uncertainty through observation geometry (Gram matrix) and demonstrating its application on $	ext{NiPS}_3$ data, culminating in adaptive experimental design strategies.
why_interesting: The rigorous quantification of parameter identifiability via geometric constraints provides a powerful systematic tool for guiding future experiments in strongly correlated materials, moving beyond simple fitting to understanding measurement limitations.
